To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dietary antioxidants, lipids and vitamin D are associated with asthma, but the evidence for clinical benefit from dietary supplementation is limited.
dietary antioxidant and PUFA intake are not associated with asthma, but maternal vitamin D intake during pregnancy may influence the development of asthma in the offspring.

(1) dietary antioxidants, vitamin D and long-chain n-6 and n-3 PUFAs have been associated with asthma in observational studies; (2) supplementation of adults with asthma and/or their children with these nutrients has minimal, if no, effect on asthma; (3) maternal intake of these nutrients has been associated with asthma development in children; and (4) further studies of the effect of maternal diet on asthma development are required.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how nutrition influences the development of asthma and allergic disease.
understanding the potential role that diet may have in influencing the prevalence and/or severity of asthma and allergic diseases.
the role that nutrition can play in determining asthma risk, particularly in early life.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is insufficient evidence at present to recommend that the public modify their dietary intake to reduce the risk of asthma.
there is no convincing evidence that diet is a major determinant of asthma.
dietary factors are unlikely to have a major influence on asthma prevalence in the general population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evidence for a role of diet in asthma is inconsistent and inconclusive.

the evidence to date suggests that maternal intake of certain nutrients during pregnancy may have a beneficial impact on childhood asthma, however, more work is needed to determine the optimal maternal diet during pregnancy to reduce the risk of childhood asthma and whether this can be achieved by supplementation.
there is a need for further research in order to determine the potential for nutrition to modify asthma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is little convincing evidence that dietary modification can prevent or reduce asthma symptoms.
there is no convincing evidence that dietary antioxidants, lipids and vitamin D have a clinically important impact on adult asthma.
there are no convincing data to support the use of dietary supplements to treat asthma in adults.
